text:
People must remember the Gen4 / Gen3 issues are even greater of a concern when you are talking the 8x bus these cards run on. If you run this on a older Gen3 platform that usually would be no problem with a 16x card like a 3060 but these being 8x cards take a much great hit on Gen3 systems. It's essentially the same bandwidth as very old Gen2 16x when you run this 8x card on Gen3 spec.

I have five of these 6600XT left and just yesterday finally replaced my last 2 B450 boards with X570 for Gen4 support and more M2 Gen4 slots. Great deals though, sold a Tomahawk B450 for $80 and bought a brand new Asus Tuf x570 for $80. Very little upgrade costs from selling off these older boards for newer. Granted some games have very little gains on Gen4. Sad they would make these 8x cards as they know plenty of people would pair these more budget ranged cards with older systems.

text:
@Blinknone  Fun fact: In the isolated bubble of the typical Nvidia user,... and average of more than 7 to 10 frames/sec better performance over AMD's offerings is "Getting Crushed," and price means almost nothing in this regard. Oddly, if AMD's card somehow beats a GeForce  card there's almost always an "excuse" for Nvidia GeForce hardware that still justifies the brand loyalty. AMD hasn't held the top performance crown since 2011. AMD cards may age like fine wine,... my XFX Radeon RX 580 GTS Black Edition 8GB card is proof of that as it's still a solid card and launched at a reasonable price for $229.00 back in 2017, but,... Nvidia users tend to upgrade more often and so rarely have the patience to wait for a card's drivers to get more polished over a 5 to 6 year period. The upgrade window for GeForce tends to be every 2 generations or so. AMD users tend to stick with a card for about 3 to four generations. Oddly Nvidia actually does a better job of driver support over longer periods of time, yet their top performance drivers typically are out by the end of the first year after a card's release. AMD takes 3 times as long to get their top performance drivers out. They are better optimized by then vs NVidia's but nobody pays attention to performance improvements within a single generation of graphics cards. It's always the next generation that sets the "new standards bar. Also in Nvidialand, Geforce cards are always better because the software is always "better", the drivers always "work", (even when they don't), content creation software is always better with Nvidia and there is always the presumption of superior quality with Nvidia. Kinda like Apple iPhones. The entry price may be much higher than the competition but there's an established sense of superior quality that builds brand loyalty. To get an Nvidia user to leave, AMD graphics cards have to more than crush Nvidia and they have to do it at the high end. Nvidia always puts out a stupidly high powered flagship card that commands a premium to get one and the next two cards are always very solid yet expensive performance segment cards. The rest of the product stack tapers off and the low end cards usually are just sufficient as display adaptors. Nvidia users with gladly pay as much as $100 or more for a GeForce card even if it only just edges out an AMD card by just a couple percentage points.

For AMD to "Crush" Nvidia, they have to utterly blow NVidia's highest end enthusiast card out of the water by a good margin and be at a price point cheaper than NVidia's mid-range cards of the same generation.
Example: It'd take the Radeon RX 7900XTX 24GB graphics card absolutely stomping the GeForce RTX 4090 Ti and do it for less than the price of the RTX 4070 Ti. Then and only then would you get Nvidia users to switch to AMD.
That's the level of brand loyalty that Nvidia has over AMD.

Nvidia marketshare is over 80% right now because of that brand loyalty.

text: I'm a bit late but what about pcie 3 performance? I heard it's locked at 8 pcie lanes
author: @ShooterUndead

text: I was looking into this recently, seems like other than one rare outlier it makes little difference (there's maybe a 2% to 5% difference at most in most games, mostly because of the PCIe 3 performance relative to PCIe 4, and not having to do with the 8x and 16x difference). In the case of Doom Eternal if you run it at the highest settings it might be limited significantly by PCIe 3 at 8x. The only explanation I've seen people suggest is that because it runs at such a high frame rate, at maximum settings it uses up the PCIe 3 bandwidth on this card. But I think they also suggested turning down the textures from the highest setting to ease up on the VRAM usage would negate this effect. In general most people seem to think it won't be much of an issue, and only one benchmark I've seen shows that negative aspect in Doom Eternal (from Hardware Unboxed). Maybe in future games it will be more relevant.

@13loodLust  The market being an oligopoly with literally two main suppliers doesnt help, but I dont think it a cartel.

Scaling up GPU production is difficult, it takes time and investment, and this is probably doubly true for the semi-conductors used. I dont think AMD and Nvidia can produce as fast they want.

text: The demand is very strong. That's why the margins have gone up. The companies are trying to meet the demand, but they can't. As they are supply limited, NVIDIA and AMD should be pricing their modules to intersect with the demand curve, sharing the increased margins with the board partners and retailers. That is the sensible thing. But they are worried about a PR backlash if they follow basic economics so they sell the cards at a price where they don't have the supply to meet the demand. Then the cards are always out of stock and still nobody is happy. The 3060 and 6600XT are priced closer to the demand curve than earlier cards in the generation. The value they represent is only in relation to current and future market conditions. How things were in the past is irrelevant. Perhaps people are priced out of the market. It sucks for those people but people should be able to bid for what they want, certainly for a hobby/luxury item like a graphics card.

text:
After having this card for two months now I can say that this card is okay at best.  First off it has a bad coil whine in games that have uncapped frame rates on menus/loading screens.  Train Simulator of all things is the worst in this regard (frames rate in the thousands! in loading screens) but was fixed by limiting the frame rate.  I don't have the fan quirks that were shown in this video.  The fans don't even turn on until the junction temperature hits 60 C where they run around 1350 RPM and goes up and down with the junction temperature.  If the junction temperature drops to 54 C they turn off.  

Control is the only raytracing game I own and it absolutely kills this card.  It's the only game I have to run at 1080p and even then the framerate still drops into the 20s at times with raytracing on.  Flight Simulator is also a rough one but it's still able to run it on ultra at 1440p over 30 fps most of the time.  Other games that I have like Resident Evil 7,  Forza Horizon 4, and GTA V can run over 100 fps on "ultra" settings although there's some stutter at times especially in Resident Evil 7.  Not sure if that's due to my older CPU (Ryzen 2700X) or because I'm on a PCIe 3 motherboard.

I think under normal market conditions this card would be $250 or perhaps even less.  At MSRP ($380 for this model) it is way overpriced and at the scalper's prices it's ridiculous.

text:
Once RDNA3 APU comes out I think AMD would prefer to abandon the entry level markets and just focus on $500+ GPU markets altogether.

This means we may see super powerful APUs but at a premium pricing than regular CPUs...

Like a RDNA3 APU with the performance of a vega 64 in it... Or a RX6600 XT.

It actually is better that way in a sense, you can save money on a GPU and PC in general with smaller ITX cases, and funnel money onto liquid cooling the APU instead of so many fans for the case.

PC cases can be as cheap as $25 for mATX and ITX sizes, and power supply requirements are tiny meaning 400-500watt PSU costs around $30-40...

author: @aaronthomas6155

text:
​ @aaronthomas6155  If you told me that one year ago, I could understand. But now, going forward, I honestly think that people not caring about RT is mostly a case of sour grapes. Nvidia gpus are at their second gen when it comes to RT acceleration, and their mid-range gpus, like the 3060/3060ti perform really well in that regard, also because of DLSS ofc. Nowadays the majority of the new games are implementing RT together with DLSS in most cases, even the smaller studios, see the game The Ascent for example.

In Q3 2021, a gpu with a 128bit bus and 8 PCIe lanes, targeting 1080p gaming, with horrid RT performances, at a $380 msrp, is an embarrassment in my opinion, a piece of trash card.

Of course we couldn't expect any RT performance progress from AMD in the current 6xxx gen, that's why, all things considered, the only thing making AMD competitive had to be the price. But It is clear that they are riding this whole shortages situation overpricing their cards because they are going to sell, one way or another.

In any case, changing the angle and playing in the position of someone who wants to buy a mid-range gpu despite the current prices situation, with the idea of keeping it for the next 3-4 years: give me a reason why I would want to choose an RX 6600XT over a 3060ti.
author: @ctrlectrld

text: @ctrlectrld  My next graphics card purchase, just like my last, will be based solely on rasterization performance.  Has nothing to do with "sour grapes"....  Out of the list of 45 games that support RTX, posted by DigitalTrends in July, I own 2 games on the list with no interest in buying any of the others.  Unless ray-tracing capability is a requirement of the next game I purchase, I still won't care about RTX.  Ray Tracing doesn't benefit the majority of the games I play therefore it adds no value to the graphics card for me.  If I could get a second RX5700 at a reasonable price (sub-$250, since it'd be used), I'd jump on it.  At $380, even with the performance, I couldn't and wouldn't recommend the RX6600XT, even for those with PCIe 4.0 support....just because of the PCIe 4.0 x8 limitation....  The memory bandwidth limitation doesn't even come into play for me, because of the PCIe limitation.  I don't care if the card needs the full bandwidth available from 16 PCIe 4.0 lanes or not, I still want the card to utilize them.  Especially at $380....
author: @aaronthomas6155

text:
@aaronthomas6155  The main thing I don't understand about the "most people don't care about RT" reasoning, is that it's not that we are sacrificing raster performance for RT, meaning: if Nvidia mid-range cards were lacking in raster vs AMD's, while performing better in RT workloads, then the reasoning would make sense. I would understand people saying "I'm gonna buy AMD because I don't care about RT". But here we're talking about similarly priced mid-range cards which have more or less equal raster performances, with Nvidia slapping great RT performances on top of it. So it's something more, at the same price. Why wouldn't you want that.

I've bought ATi/AMD my whole life: at comparable performances, with both CPUs and GPUs, I prefer going with AMD. In this specific case tho', talking about mid-range, I am not really liking AMD's attitude. They act like they are on top of the GPU market, while they are not. I prefer AMD yes, but my own interests will always have the priority. I always bought mid-range because it's more than ok for the level of gaming I do, if Nvidia will give me more for the same price, I won't bat an eye and go with them. I don't get people putting a multi billion company interests before their own. $250 for an RX5700 would be a great deal, here in Germany they go for 600 bucks sadly. I can get a new 3060ti for that price.

@Gamers Nexus - So Steve let me get this straight.... RTX 2080 level performance for 380$ is a bad deal? ... Really..... So essentially half-ish of the RTX 2080 launch price of 699$..... That's not fucking stagnation dude! That's probably one of the largest generational gaps we've ever seen!!! Like seriously show me a larger one in "the age of 3D graphics"! ... I've been in this "game" since I was 4 and I'm 41 now - and I'm having a HARD time thinking of anything (in comparison - I picked up a free computer the other day - infinite value! LOL) which is ACTUALLY better value than the 3060, 3060 TI, the 6600 XT - and what the 3050 and 3050 TI looks to be if any of the leaks are correct. YES I know that you could buy a flagship GPU for 500$ a decade ago - however this is by no means an apples to apples comparison. There is inflation, the more expensive components on the board and a more "limited" market. We used to have S3, Matrox, Nvidia, 3DFX, ATI and so on. Realistically right now we have 2 - AMD and Nvidia. Sure Intel is coming but... they ain't here yet! This means RnD is more expensive. There used to be a bunch of smaller manufactures of components, however now the availability of "new/more advanced" components has been limited because of the - well limited market. You bring up the memory - sure that's really expensive these days - but what about stuff like the (e.g.) power delivery system on a modern card? Modern cards go apeshit if the power isn't "clean" enough so... stuff like that adds cost! The fact that you can actually get this much power compared to last gen for 350-399$ is actually pretty damn good all things considered. It means you can build a 900$ "high-ish" 5600X gaming system. AND - Let's be real here - non of the people considering buying a card like this owns a 1000$ 4k 144hz gaming monitor.

Listen I know these cards are not "exciting" in comparison ... just like a Kia Ceed isn't exciting compared to a Dodge Viper however it's ACTUALLY a really good car!... and just like with many "cheaper" cars have become better quality - the quality these new GPUs deliver is ACTUALLY a premium experience. Yes you can get something faster - but why? ANYONE on a budget should forget about the 1000$ class of cards - especially when you can get this much power for less than 400$. Outside of benchmarks - do you seriously believe that these cards will be any less enjoyable for 99% of all gamers on their 1080p or 1440p monitors? text:
@aaronthomas6155  I know "how this shit works". Standard inelastic demand situation where price changes don't result in a decrease in demand because perceived utility of the object is not diminished. So, yeah I can agree half-way. 
But, prices aren't solely affected by consumers. Economic and political forces, the cost of parts and mfg. cost differences, market conditions, and competitive pricing by other suppliers contribute, too. Supply shortages and high demand could possibly affect prices. And there is certainly no desire to raise prices to improve the bottom line; no company would try to maximize profits.
But, lets say that it is accurate; it doesn't mean that the pricing isn't set in such a way that buying this part is a very poor choice when other competitive options exist for less, which clearly marks how out of alignment the pricing for this product is at MSRP or higher. Consumers may exacerbate high prices, but AMD is setting prices - prices which don't necessarily make sense when viewed across the competitive landscape.


Still, it is a good idea. Just need everyone only ever buy reasonable things at reasonable prices.

text:
@timothygibney159  Technology that is not cutting edge is what gets cheaper. As newer tech comes out, the price goes up because state of the art tech = more difficult to make = more expensive. Look at LEDs for example. Regular simple LEDs are cheap therefore easy to make because of economies of scale and they're not new. More are made = high supply+steady/low demand = low prices. This does not apply to super-high quality or high-build-price LEDs like for powerful flashlights or ones made for color correcting as those are more difficult to make.

In the GPU world, as the cost-per-transistor goes down, they just pack more transistors in a particular size and the size goes up, so price goes up as a result, along with extreme demand now that everyone wants a PC, extreme demand + slow economies of scale due to covid = low supply, and low supply + high demand = high prices. Price isn't regulated because this stuff is considered luxury goods, not utility, therefore subject to free pricing. This is why consumer CPU prices haven't gone down over the years (except HEDT/server cause Intel doesn't have a leg up anymore to overcharge) along with stuff like upper end motherboards or other components. Consoles get lucky because they sell at a loss for tens of millions of units cause the real profit margins for them is software (games, subscription services, DLCs, microtransactions, etc).

text:
@timothygibney159  I went the other way. Last November I managed to snag two RX 5600 XT's for £248 each from a local trade supplier, one for me and one for my daughter. I was upgrading from an RX580 and GTX970 respectively. The cards were instantly sold out just minutes after I'd bought that pair. Then I got to thinking and watching. So five days later the same supplier came into six more of the cards and I bought them all for £276 each. I hadn't sold on our old cards yet, so I kept the RX580 for my machine, installed one of the 5600 XT's in my daughters machine and sold all the other seven 5600 XT's for £450 each.

I too have a 4K screen, an LG TV in fact, but I am quite happy running games at 1080p or even lower - they don't looks so bad - and I hit over 100fps with an RX580. I did some testing with one of the 5600 XT's and it played lots of games at 1440p perfectly well - north of 60fps. Radeon 6600 XT:    PCIe 4.0  x8   =  16 GB/s  =  Enough
Radeon 6600 XT:    PCIe 3.0  x8   =    8 GB/s  =  Potential performance hit!

Radeon 5700 XT:     PCIe 4.0 x16  =  32 GB/s  =  Way more than enough
Radeon 5700 XT:     PCIe 4.0 x8    =  16 GB/s  =  Enough
Radeon 5700 XT:     PCIe 3.0 x16  =  16 GB/s  =  Enough
Radeon 5700 XT:     PCIe 4.0 x4    =    8 GB/s  =  Potential performance hit!
Radeon 5700 XT:     PCIe 3.0 x8    =    8 GB/s  =  Potential performance hit!


Requirements for PCIe 4.0:
  - Motherboard supports it (AMD: X570, B550, Intel: Z590, B560, ...)
  - CPU supports it (AMD Zen 2, Intel 11th Gen Core)
  - GPU supports it (GeForce RTX 30 -series, Radeon 5000/6000).

If all of those requirements aren't met, PCIe 3.0 will be used. Thus halving the speed. More specifically, halving the maximum speed of that PCIe connector.

text:
​ @CanIHasThisName  Overall the transfer speed of the memory is faster on the 3060, due to having a larger bus width. The size of the memory bus alongside the effective memory clock are the two of the components that you use when calculating total VRAM memory bandwidth (or overall speed). The equations used for GDDR6 are:
Memory clock x2 (rise and fall) x4 (quad data rate) = Effective memory clock (in MB/s, ÷ by 1000 for GB/s)
Effective memory clock x Memory bus width ÷8 = Memory bandwidth (total transfer speed)
So:
RTX 3060 = Memory clock of 1875Mhz. Effective memory clock = (1875 x2) x4 = 15GB/s.
15GB/s on a 192-bit bus = (15 x 192) ÷ 8 = 360. Which gives it a total bandwidth of 360GB/s.

6600XT = Memory clock of 2000Mhz. Effective memory clock = (2000 x2) x4 = 16GB/s.
16GB/s on a 128-bit bus = (16 x 128) ÷ 8 = 256. Which gives it a total bandwidth of 256GB/s.

The 3060's memory amount is not only 50% larger than the 6600XT, but it's memory bandwidth is also 33% faster.

text:
@samhammoud4315  
"How in the world is this worth $200?"
Well its simple Sam, this card is a replacement for a 200 dollar card, in every way possible really.  From where it falls on FPS in games compared to other video cards both produced and not produced by AMD, too the quality of parts used.  It is the new version of the RX 5600, and when you trace it back to when most of the people started buying video cards you see the card this one falls in line with was the RX-400 series and it seems people are comparing it too the RX-480 which is wrong by naming at least, because this would be the RX 460 which I believe had a MSRP of about 86 dollars lol.  I wish I were kidding there, but that is something I hope some people dig into a bit more. 

"Have you seen the prices of slower and older cards. 1660 is being sold for the same price"
Yes they have, and that is exactly what people are up in arms about really.  I like to try to compare markets a bit, as it gives us a better understanding when something is really really wrong with a market. 
Look at the Fender Squire electric guitars, that market is strange as well.  I could go to a store and buy a brand new Fender Squire Bullet guitar for less than 100 dollars at one point, I mean those things were cheap and always at least functional for the most part.  Now days If I go to buy a Fender Squire Bullet guitar, I can expect to pay 190 ish dollars..  I say Ish there because the actual price is 189.99 plus tax, which means I would likely have to pay over 200 dollars, that when I started playing would have cost me less than a hundred for.  See something wrong with that? Perhaps your going to jump in with "Inflation" or something right?  Well between the time I started and now, inflation as only actually added 20 or so dollars to the cost of that guitar.  So what about the other 60 to 80 dollars? where do you think that came from?   
Its not that is more expensive to build the guitar, because in reality where we all live, factory's have automated more and more of the process, which means less labor cost and more production and of course more consistency between guitars.  Shipping cost are low when you ship in massive bulk like that, and thus its cheaper to ship now then it ever has been..  So that means the guitar should be cheaper than it is, and by a lot. 
Now you may wonder, what does guitars have to do with GPU's?  well in this case we are comparing price hikes over time, and when we compare the percentage of price hikes we see something danged odd.  GPU's have actually increased in price at MSRP more so than guitars.  With guitars we see a 40 plus percent increase in price ish depending on the model and manufacturer, some goes up as high as 80% and for the same exact product.   But when we look at GPU's, we see a minimum of 100 percent increase in price at MSRP, and just like guitars that price hike has nothing to do with inflation really.  I mean we all accept inflation, we hate it of course, but we accept it.  What we do not accept is the people in charge of these company's increasing there profit margins, while outright lying to us as to the cost to produce there products.   
We consumers are not buying products one or two steps further down the supply chain when compared to where we were, we are buying at the same points.  So if someone got there video card at Best Buy some 10 years ago, they are likely buying from Best buy now.  Or at the very least, they are buying form a company that is exactly the same amount of company's removed from AMD or NVIDIA or whom ever.  So we can't accept the idea that its just yet another new company getting between us and the products.   Since its cheaper per capita to produce these items, we can't accept the lie that its not cheaper, or in some kind of up slope due to the process node being smaller, because that is just not how reality works.  If it was cheaper for a company to go from using 20nm chips down to 16nm chips, and every process node shrink before that, then there is no reason to think it cost them just so much more to produce these 10nm chips or even at some point 4nm chips..  
Put it to you this way, that excuse is kind of like saying that its easier to lift 20 pounds than it is to life 30, but its harder to life 10 pounds than it is 20 pounds..  Logically you know its just not the case lol.  Sorry, I saw that argued in this thread, not by you mind you, but I wanted to put my thoughts in order on that one a bit, and decided to use you as a sound board lol.

Now, taking the side of the consumer means you will always push for better deals for the consumer on these things.  It is only better for the company's for us to pretend these prices are okay, and that can only ever be the case.  It is always better, to push the people in charge of these company's to make the price of there goods cheaper, from the perspective of the consumer.   Where we all agree a profit is okay, we do not all agree that profit can be what ever insane amount a group of folks running a company pretend is the norm.   For many years in our country, company's would be outright punished by our government if they charged more than 10 percent past cost, and now days the norm is 40 percent past cost.. at least that is the norm people pretend is being done, now days its more like 100 percent or more, depending on how strong the monopoly or Cartel is on that market.   ..  See I am doing it again, I am going deeper than I need to. 
I hope all is well, good day and good luck :)

@natma relnam 
what happens when people decide the price is too high?  Answer, the price goes down.  Looks like I am dressed for the job I have, not the job I am pretending to have huh. 
This card in fact is not a 300 + tariffs card, it is a 75 dollar with tariffs card, that is being sold for multiple times its actual worth.  In the end, this card should be being sold for around a hundred dollars.  There are many reasons why this is happening, but the price to make the card and tariffs are not one of them. 
First there is greed, why make a decent profit, when I can make extreme profit.  Second is marketing.  If I can fool the buyer into thinking this is a acceptable price, he/she will spend as much as I can get him/her to spend.  Then on the end of the buyer there is the fact that people are ignorant enough to accept the lies they are fed.  As a example, "there is a shortage on raw material."  When the material in the chips is the second most abundant resource on Earth, I call foul.  Lets not forget the excuse, "We had to shut down manufacturing for the shut downs, we don't have enough cards."  This is a funny one, because within a month of production, they had already made up for the loss in numbers that they racked up during the lock downs. 
See what I am getting at?  First, they try a price, and we get to accept that price or not, if enough of us do not accept the price, they drop the price, until we do.  This process has broken down a bit, because people are forgetting what side of this they are on.  You just defended the supplier, when you are a consumer.  Our job as consumers is to 1, keep them honest, and 2, get the best price possible.  Accepting a 400 dollar price tag, on a item that is worth 100 dollars is in fact bad for consumers, thus it is bad for you.

Price wise, it's a little uncomfortable, even though I got the 3060 at near to MSRP.   I might have prefered an MSRP 3070 or 3080, but the crypto market determines that this is not possible.

text:
@olaole8315  a big reason why fsr can be dlss like is the fact that at 4k ultra quality it running at 1662p which is a fair bit higher than 1440p and then it'll improve the image a little nicer and further more give you a sharpening filter to further make you believe it looks better but it doesn't add in detail that wasn't there and honestly native 1440p does a good job as is. 

But heres the thing you can drop to 1080p and the image looks fine but drop to 800p and below while using taa of which fsr relies on taa when available (it gives the best result), makes taa stronger then what it'll do is add its own blurring ontop while looking for edges which won't be nearly as defined as you have this horrible taa smeared 800p image being further destroyed.

At lower resolutions you straight up need temporal upscaling to attempt to get a reasonable image as you get very little info and temporal upscaling pulls alot of its data over frames aka time even if it has to be taa upscaling it'll do a much much better job as despite it having huge glaring artifacts it'll be reasonable to look at and you'll be able to see whats going on even if itd be a little painful if youve experienced alot better. There's loads of info to back this up on the Internet. 

Just so you're aware using taa to upscale doesn't equate to just adding more taa onto an image, 1 is also building non aliasing focused detail onto an image while the other only really focuses on aliasing.

But...Inflation; the value of the Dollar isn't static, and with transportation and manufacturing increases across the board and the Dollar losing measurable value almost by the day now, why wouldn't video cards increase in price by the roughly 15% average that every other new product has since March?

In this economy, even a price comparison to new cards from six months ago is apples to oranges since manufacturers can't take the hit of changing the MSRP on already existing cards that they may now be making no margin...or even taking a loss...on, but they CAN ensure they actually make their margin on new launches.

IS mining a factor at purchase (not MSRP)? Yes...yes it is.

Is Mining a factor driving up MSRPs? No...not really for the most part (•cough• Nvidia •cough•).

text: @digitalis2977  Mining isn't directly a factor, but final sales price is.  Sales trends are always a factor in determining MSRP of a new product in an established market.
